heading: Dabu: Rajasthan's hand-applied mud-resist print

p: Dabu (also written daboo) is a mud-resist printing technique from Rajasthan, practised in places such as Akola, Bagru and around Jaipur. The word comes from "dabana", to press, because the resist is pressed onto the cloth with carved wooden blocks.
Instead of printing colour, the printer prints a paste that keeps colour out. Wherever the paste sits, the dye cannot reach, so the pattern appears in the base colour after dyeing.

list: A paste is prepared from black clay, gum, lime and wheat husk, and left to settle.
The printer presses the paste onto the fabric with a hand-carved block, motif by motif.
Sawdust is sprinkled over the wet paste so it does not smudge, and the cloth is dried in the sun.
The fabric is dyed, very often in indigo, then the mud is washed away to reveal the design.
For deeper effects the process can be repeated, with more resist and a second dyeing.

p: As the mud dries it develops tiny cracks. A little dye seeps into these cracks, leaving fine veins across the pattern. This soft, crackled look is the signature of dabu and cannot be copied exactly by machine, so every metre is slightly different.

list: Hand wash in cold water with a mild soap, separately for the first few washes.
Dry in shade and iron on the reverse side.

faq: What is the difference between dabu and regular block print?
In regular block printing the block carries colour onto the cloth. In dabu the block carries a mud paste that blocks the dye, so the design shows in the base colour after dyeing.
Why does dabu have fine lines through the pattern?
The mud resist cracks as it dries, and a little dye enters the cracks. These veins are the natural signature of hand-done dabu.
Indigo is the most traditional colour for dabu, but it is also dyed in other colours such as rust, green and mustard.
Will two dabu pieces look identical?
No. Because the paste, the cracks and the dyeing are all done by hand, every piece has small differences.
